target.name: Orc1 removal from chromatin
target.description: Eukaryotic cells must fire each replication origin exactly once per cycle, and displacing Orc1 from chromatin after origins have fired is one of the safeguards that enforces this. Once S phase begins, cyclin A–CDK2 phosphorylates Orc1, which is released from the origin recognition complex bound at chromatin and targeted for ubiquitination by an SCF-type cullin–RING ligase built on CUL1, RBX1 and SKP1 with the SKP2 substrate receptor, then degraded by the 26S proteasome.

[untitled BTM module] These genes converge on the regulation of gene expression at the steps between transcription and protein turnover. Cyclin T2 partners CDK9 in the elongation kinase that releases paused RNA polymerase II, while cyclin C works within the Mediator kinase module that gates promoter engagement, and ARID4A and SP3 act on chromatin and promoter DNA to set which genes are read.

[untitled BTM module] This grouping centres on transcriptional repression and chromatin-based silencing, the machinery that keeps developmental and proliferative genes switched off until they are needed. Polycomb components are the anchor: BMI1 is a core subunit of the PRC1 ubiquitin ligase complex that marks histone H2A to maintain silencing, while AEBP2 is a zinc-finger accessory factor that helps target the companion PRC2 methyltransferase to chromatin.

target.name: Evasion of Oncogene Induced Senescence Due to Defective p16INK4A binding to CDK4 and CDK6
target.description: Cells that acquire an activating oncogenic lesion normally respond by arresting permanently rather than proliferating, and p16INK4A is one of the brakes that enforces that arrest. Encoded by CDKN2A, it binds CDK4 and CDK6 and blocks their cyclin D-dependent phosphorylation of RB, holding the cell at the G1 restriction point and locking in the senescent state.
